newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kirch says reports of pay-TV losses exaggerated.
newsitem.headline: Kirch says reports of pay-TV losses exaggerated.

text.p: German media group Kirch dismissed as wildly exaggerated speculation reports that its infant digital pay-television service DF1 would run up start-up costs of several billion marks.

Gottfried Zmeck, managing director of the firm controlled by media mogul Leo Kirch, told Reuters DF1 was still expected to be in the black by the year 2000 or shortly thereafter, with costs still estimated at around one billion marks.

Even if the turn to profit were delayed a year or two, this would "definitely not" mean financial problems for Kirch, Zmeck said. The higher estimates of DF1 costs were being circulated in part by "interested parties."

CS First Boston media expert Christopher Renaud has estimated DF1 costs at up to 3.8 billion marks. Meanwhile Germany's Spiegel magazine, using figures compiled by Kirch's main rival Bertelsmann, this weekend said DF1 could face costs of up to six billion marks.
"Much of that can be read in terms of building up a negotiating position," commented Zmeck on the Spiegel article.
Bertelsmann, co-owner of the established pay-TV channel Premiere, is thought to be negotiating with Kirch over integrating Premiere with the DF1 digital platform.
Zmeck said there had been "contacts" with Bertelsmann. Asked if he expected an agreement soon, he simply said: "I don't know."

Kirch holds a 25 percent stake in Premiere, but opted last year to strike out on his own with DF1 after a bitter row over standards for decoder systems. Bertelsmann and Canal Plus each own 37.5 percent of Premiere.

DF1 has fallen far short of its goals in its initial months. Zmeck said the service now had well over 30,000 clients, but that is far off Kirch's target of amassing 700,000 subscribers by the end of this year.

But Zmeck said he was sticking to this year's subscriber goal. Should the company manage to strike a deal with Deutsche Telekom over the use of its cable network, subscriber numbers could surge, he predicted.

Kirch has been at the centre of massive controversy in the past week after details emerged of a huge credit line which had been extended to it by banks including a loan agency controlled by the state of Bavaria.

On Friday, Kirch issued a statement saying it had decided not to take up the loan because of the controversy. Rivals and trade unions had labelled the loan a form of state subsidy, which Kirch flatly denied.
